sheffield.intro: Sheffield maps two street trees, and both are here because people refused to let them go. The Chelsea Road Elm in Nether Edge, a rare Huntingdon elm and a breeding tree for the white-letter hairstreak butterfly, survived a four-year fight with the city's felling contract. The Vernon Oak in Dore, a field boundary tree that the suburb grew up around, was climbed by a protester in 2017 and kept in 2018. Both stand on public pavements, free to see at any hour.
sheffield.meta_description: Two Sheffield street trees saved by campaigners: the Chelsea Road Elm, a butterfly tree in Nether Edge, and the 150-year-old Vernon Oak in Dore.
sheffield.question_meta: Sheffield's oldest mapped tree is the Vernon Oak in Dore, put at about 150 years old, a street tree kept after a long campaign.
sheffield.question_answer: Sheffield's oldest mapped tree is the Vernon Oak, a street oak on Vernon Road in Dore that Trees for Cities put at about 150 years old in 2018. The city's other mapped tree, the Chelsea Road Elm in Nether Edge, is a little younger, at roughly 120 to 130 years.
sheffield.question_context: Both trees owe their survival to the same argument. Under a long highways contract, Sheffield felled street trees in large numbers, and residents began to resist, standing under trees, blocking the work and taking the case to the press. The Chelsea Road Elm became one of the best-known cases. It is a Huntingdon elm, a hybrid that has resisted Dutch elm disease, and one of roughly a thousand mature elms left in the UK outside Brighton and Edinburgh. White-letter hairstreak butterflies breed on it, Butterfly Conservation spoke up for it, and it was runner-up in the Woodland Trust's Tree of the Year in 2016. It was saved in 2019. The Vernon Oak began as a field boundary tree before the houses of Dore were built around it; a protester climbed it in 2017, and the council agreed to keep it after changing course in 2018. Neither tree has a precise pin, and the most recent sightings we can cite are 2023 for the elm and 2018 for the oak, so a reader's photograph of either is welcome.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Sheffield?
faq.a: The Vernon Oak on Vernon Road in Dore, put at about 150 years old in 2018. It began as a field boundary tree before the suburb grew up around it.

faq.q: Why is the Chelsea Road Elm famous?
faq.a: It is a rare disease-resistant Huntingdon elm that hosts the white-letter hairstreak butterfly, and residents fought for about four years to stop it being felled. It was saved in 2019.

faq.q: Can you visit Sheffield's trees for free?
faq.a: Yes. Both are street trees on public pavements, visible at any time with no gate or ticket.

ripon.intro: Ripon's mapped tree stands in the deer park at Studley Royal, a short walk from the ruins of Fountains Abbey. It is a sweet chestnut that the National Trust calls a pre-18th-century pollard, cut back at head height for its wood, and it faces St Mary's Church, William Burges's Victorian church, across the drive. It sits on the Trust's own ancient trees walk, among chestnuts planted around 1710 and an avenue of limes, so the walk to it passes other old trees too.
ripon.meta_description: A sweet chestnut pollard older than 1700 in the Studley Royal deer park near Ripon, opposite Burges's St Mary's Church, on the National Trust's tree walk.
ripon.question_meta: Ripon's oldest mapped tree is a sweet chestnut pollard in the Studley Royal deer park, which the National Trust dates to before the 18th century.
ripon.question_answer: Ripon's oldest mapped tree is the pollard sweet chestnut by St Mary's Church in the Studley Royal deer park, which the National Trust describes as a pre-18th-century pollard. It stands beside the drive opposite the church, about 4 miles from Ripon.
ripon.question_context: Studley Royal is the National Trust estate that holds the ruins of Fountains Abbey and an 18th-century water garden, and its deer park is open to walkers. The Trust publishes an ancient trees walk through the park, and this chestnut is one of its stops. Pollarding meant cutting a tree above the reach of browsing animals so it would regrow a crop of poles, a working practice that often lengthens a tree's life, and in a deer park the height mattered. The Trust dates the hillside chestnuts nearby to around 1710 and calls this one older than that. Across the drive stands St Mary's Church, built in the 1870s to designs by William Burges, which the Trust calls his masterpiece. Everything known about the tree comes from the Trust's walk; no girth or closer age has been published, so if you visit and measure it, tell us. Reach it on foot from the Fountains Abbey visitor centre in 15 to 20 minutes, through the pedestrian gate into the deer park.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree near Ripon?
faq.a: The pollard sweet chestnut opposite St Mary's Church in the Studley Royal deer park, described by the National Trust as older than the 18th century.

faq.q: Do you need a ticket to see it?
faq.a: The deer park is open to walkers, and the tree is on the Trust's public ancient trees walk. The deer park car park is pay and display, free to members; the abbey and water garden have their own entry terms.

faq.q: How do you get there from Ripon?
faq.a: It is about 4 miles by footpath, or 15 to 20 minutes on foot from the Fountains Abbey visitor centre.

defynnog.intro: Defynnog maps one tree, and the arguments about it are as big as the tree. The great yew of St Cynog's churchyard grows from a low mound as nine stems with a combined girth of about 11 metres. A certificate in the village says 5,000 years; Wikipedia leans to 2,000 to 3,000; the Ancient Yew Group sets a minimum of 1,300. A second yew five metres away is its genetic twin. Free, in the Brecon Beacons National Park.
defynnog.meta_description: The Defynnog Yew in a Brecon Beacons churchyard: nine stems, about 11 metres round, its age argued from 1,300 years to 5,000. Free to visit.
defynnog.question_meta: Defynnog's oldest tree is the Defynnog Yew in St Cynog's churchyard, its age disputed from a 1,300-year minimum to a claimed 5,000.
defynnog.question_answer: Defynnog's oldest and only mapped tree is the Defynnog Yew, a European Yew (Taxus baccata) in the churchyard of St Cynog's Church, near Sennybridge in Powys. Its age is disputed. A certificate signed by David Bellamy says about 5,000 years, Wikipedia calls 2,000 to 3,000 more likely, and the Ancient Yew Group sets a minimum of 1,300.
defynnog.question_context: The tree rises from a mound about eight metres across and a metre high, as nine stems with a combined girth of about 11 metres; the Ancient Yew Group measured 11.58 metres in 1998. A second yew roughly five metres west on the north side of the church has been shown by DNA to be genetically identical, perhaps grown from a branch that touched the ground and rooted, while the two yews on the south side are separate trees. Both pairs are female, and every one of them is classed as ancient. In 2014 newspapers repeated the 5,000 figure and called it Britain's oldest tree, a title several Welsh yews are given and none can prove; Llangernyw's yew, to the north, is another. St Cynog's is a Grade I listed church, mostly Norman and 15th century, with an ogham and Latin inscribed stone in its porch, and graves have been dug between the two northern yews. Look on the smaller tree for a patch of albino leaves. The TrawsCymru T6 bus between Brecon and Swansea stops in the village.

faq.q: How old is the Defynnog Yew?
faq.a: Nobody knows. Claims run from a 1,300-year minimum set by the Ancient Yew Group, through Wikipedia's 2,000 to 3,000, to the 5,000 years on a 2002 certificate.

faq.q: Is it Britain's oldest tree?
faq.a: That claim was made in the press in 2014, but no one has proved it, and other yews, Llangernyw among them, carry the same claim. We make it for none of them.

faq.q: Can you visit it for free?
faq.a: Yes. It stands in the open churchyard of St Cynog's, and the T6 bus between Brecon and Swansea stops in Defynnog.

discoed.intro: Discoed maps one tree: the great yew north of St Michael's Church, in a quiet corner of Radnorshire near Presteigne. Popular opinion makes it Wales's oldest yew, at 5,000 years, a figure even the guides that repeat it doubt. Measured, it is 9.68 metres round, with a second ancient yew beside it. The church was first mentioned in 1291, and a spring at the gate is now a well. Free and open.
discoed.meta_description: The Discoed Yew near Presteigne: 9.68 metres round, popularly called 5,000 years old with no proof. Free, in St Michael's churchyard.
discoed.question_meta: Discoed's oldest tree is the great yew of St Michael's churchyard, popularly called 5,000 years old, a claim nobody has proved.
discoed.question_answer: Discoed's oldest and only mapped tree is the Discoed Yew, a European Yew (Taxus baccata) north of St Michael's Church near Presteigne in Powys. Local opinion calls it about 5,000 years old, but that figure rests on size graphs rather than evidence, and its real age is not documented.
discoed.question_context: The 5,000-year figure goes back to Allen Meredith, who estimated the ages of yews from graphs of their size, and the monument guide Wondermondo, while repeating it, says no one knows it for sure and that it is most likely not true. Several Welsh yews carry rival claims to be the oldest, and we back none of them. The measurements disagree too. The Ancient Yew Group recorded 9.68 metres at 90 centimetres in 1998; another published figure is 11.28 metres, and a 1994 gazetteer gave 22 feet. A hollow, irregular yew rarely measures the same way twice. A second ancient yew in the churchyard is 6.71 metres round, and a third notable yew stands by the lane to the car park. St Michael's is first mentioned in 1291, and a spring at the churchyard gate has become a well. Discoed has no railway or regular bus; it is about 5 km west of Presteigne. Our most recent record of the tree is not recent, so a visitor's photograph is welcome.

faq.q: How old is the Discoed Yew?
faq.a: Not documented. It is popularly called 5,000 years old, but that figure comes from size graphs, and the guides that repeat it doubt it.

faq.q: How big is it?
faq.a: The Ancient Yew Group measured 9.68 metres round in 1998; other sources give up to 11.28 metres, since a hollow yew is hard to measure the same way twice.

faq.q: How do you get to Discoed?
faq.a: There is no railway or regular bus. Discoed is about 5 km west of Presteigne, a short drive or about an hour on foot.

pennant-melangell.intro: Pennant Melangell maps a ring of yews around the round churchyard of St Melangell's shrine church, at the head of a dead-end valley in the Berwyn hills. Six yews grow here, four of them ancient, the largest 8.71 metres round. The church puts them at 2,000 years, an estimate rather than a measurement. Burial pits at the site go back to between 1500 and 1000 BC. Free, and four miles up a lane from Llangynog.
pennant-melangell.meta_description: Ancient yews ring the round churchyard of St Melangell's shrine church in the Berwyn hills, said to be 2,000 years old. Free, remote.
pennant-melangell.question_meta: Pennant Melangell's oldest trees are the ancient yews around St Melangell's churchyard, which the church estimates at 2,000 years old.
pennant-melangell.question_answer: Pennant Melangell's oldest trees are the yews ringing the circular churchyard of St Melangell's shrine church, four of them ancient, the largest 8.71 metres round. The church estimates them at about 2,000 years old, a figure the National Churches Trust repeats; it is an estimate, not a measurement.
pennant-melangell.question_context: The churchyard is round, and that shape is old. Burial pits found at the church site have been carbon-dated to between 1500 and 1000 BC, long before the 12th-century shrine church that now stands at its centre. St Melangell, by her legend, sheltered a hunted hare under her cloak and faced down a prince and his hounds, and she is the patron saint of hares. Six yews grow around the wall, four of them large and ancient, measuring 8.71, 7.16, 6.71 and 5.44 metres in the Ancient Yew Group's records. The 2,000-year figure is the church's; others note that certificates have dated some Welsh yews to only 500 to 800 years, so the honest range is wide. Treat the ring as one place to stand rather than hunting for a single trunk. The church sits about four miles up a narrow valley road from Llangynog, with no bus or railway to the door. Buses reach Llangynog from Oswestry, and from there the walk up the valley is part of the visit.

faq.q: How old are the Pennant Melangell yews?
faq.a: The church estimates about 2,000 years, and the National Churches Trust gives the same figure. It is an estimate; no measured age exists, and some Welsh yews certified that old have been put at 500 to 800 years.

faq.q: Why is the churchyard round?
faq.a: It is an ancient enclosure. Burial pits at the site have been carbon-dated to between 1500 and 1000 BC, long before the 12th-century church.

faq.q: How do you get there?
faq.a: By car or on foot. The church is about four miles up a dead-end valley road from Llangynog; buses reach Llangynog from Oswestry.

llanerfyl.intro: Llanerfyl maps one tree: a yew in St Erfyl's churchyard that looks like four trunks standing in a ring and is reported to be a single tree, 10.67 metres around all four. Lewis's Topographical Dictionary called it one of the finest yews in Wales, and an 1872 account named it the mother yew of Montgomeryshire. Legend says it grew from St Padarn's staff. A fifth or sixth century stone found beneath it is now in the church. Free.
llanerfyl.meta_description: The Llanerfyl Yew in Powys: four trunks in a ring, 10.67 metres around, said to be one tree grown from St Padarn's staff. Free churchyard.
llanerfyl.question_meta: Llanerfyl's oldest tree is the yew in St Erfyl's churchyard, four trunks in a ring reported to be one tree; its age is not measured.
llanerfyl.question_answer: Llanerfyl's oldest and only mapped tree is the Llanerfyl Yew, a European Yew (Taxus baccata) in St Erfyl's churchyard on the A458 west of Welshpool. It grows as four trunks in a ring, 10.67 metres around all four. The age often quoted, about 1,400 years, rests on legend rather than measurement.
llanerfyl.question_context: Its trunks stand in a circle inside a low wall, three of them recorded as female and one as male, and DNA work is reported to show that the trunks are one organism. The Ancient Yew Group recorded it as a single ancient tree in 1998. It has been admired for centuries. Lewis's Topographical Dictionary of Wales called it one of the finest yew-trees in the principality, and an 1872 account named it the mother yew of Montgomeryshire. Its legend says St Padarn left his staff, Cyrwen, here in the late sixth or early seventh century, and the yew grew from it. That story is where the 1,400-year figure comes from, so we call the tree ancient and leave the number open. Something old certainly lay beneath it. In 1915 a stone inscribed in the fifth or sixth century was removed from under the yew, and it is on display inside the church. Buses along the A458 are infrequent, so most visitors come by car, about half an hour from Welshpool.

faq.q: How old is the Llanerfyl Yew?
faq.a: Not measured. The figure of about 1,400 years comes from the legend of St Padarn's staff, so the honest answer is ancient, age unknown.

faq.q: Is it one tree or four?
faq.a: It grows as four trunks in a ring, but DNA work is reported to show they are a single organism, 10.67 metres around all four.

faq.q: Is it free to visit?
faq.a: Yes. It stands in the open churchyard of St Erfyl's in the village of Llanerfyl, on the A458.

gresford.intro: Gresford maps one tree: the great yew of All Saints' churchyard, 8.99 metres round and, by the Ancient Yew Group's reckoning, older than the 13th-century part of the church. Wikipedia's account of the church says it was already ancient when Richard II ordered yews planted for longbows. Thirty-three younger yews share the churchyard. The village is in the Seven Wonders of Wales rhyme for its bells, not its tree. Free, near Wrexham.
gresford.meta_description: The Gresford Yew near Wrexham: 8.99 metres round, older than the 13th-century church beside it, among 33 younger yews. Free churchyard.
gresford.question_meta: Gresford's oldest tree is the Gresford Yew in All Saints' churchyard, older than the church's 13th-century fabric; no measured age exists.
gresford.question_answer: Gresford's oldest and only mapped tree is the Gresford Yew, a European Yew (Taxus baccata) in All Saints' churchyard, Gresford, near Wrexham. The Ancient Yew Group says it is certainly older than the 13th-century part of the church and measured it at 8.99 metres round in 1999. Nobody has published a measured age.
gresford.question_context: All Saints' churchyard holds 34 yews, and only one of them is ancient by the Ancient Yew Group's standard. The other 33 are younger trees, which makes the great one easy to pick out at nearly nine metres round. The church counts its yews among its remarkable features, and Wikipedia's account of All Saints' says this tree was already ancient when Richard II ordered yews planted for longbows in the 14th century. Beyond that its age is guesswork, and round numbers attached to it are not ones we can trace to a firm source, so ancient is the honest word. Gresford appears in the old rhyme of the Seven Wonders of Wales, but for its church bells, not its yew. The village is also known for the Gresford colliery disaster of 1934, in which 266 men died underground, and the yew was already old then. Buses between Wrexham and Chester stop in Gresford, and the churchyard is open and free.

faq.q: How old is the Gresford Yew?
faq.a: No measured age exists. The Ancient Yew Group says it is certainly older than the 13th-century part of All Saints' Church.

faq.q: Is the Gresford Yew one of the Seven Wonders of Wales?
faq.a: No. The rhyme names Gresford's church bells. The yew stands in the same churchyard.

faq.q: How do you get there?
faq.a: Buses between Wrexham and Chester stop in Gresford, a short walk from All Saints'. The churchyard is free and open.

nevern.intro: Nevern maps one tree, and people come for the colour of it. The bleeding yew, second on the right of the avenue to St Brynach's church, weeps a dark red-brown sap from a broken stub, and the Ancient Yew Group says it draws thousands of visitors a year. The avenue itself is of no great age. The churchyard's older treasures are a carved Celtic cross of around the year 1000 and an ogham-inscribed stone. Free, near Newport, Pembrokeshire.
nevern.meta_description: The Bleeding Yew of Nevern weeps dark red sap in St Brynach's churchyard, Pembrokeshire, beside a Celtic cross. Free to visit, near Newport.
nevern.question_meta: Nevern's most famous tree is the Bleeding Yew in St Brynach's churchyard; its age is not documented, though the avenue is said to be 600 to 700.
nevern.question_answer: Nevern's mapped tree is the Bleeding Yew, a European Yew (Taxus baccata) in St Brynach's churchyard near Newport, Pembrokeshire, the second yew on the right of the avenue to the church door. It weeps a dark red-brown sap from a broken stub. Its age is not documented.
nevern.question_context: The Ancient Yew Group does not class the Nevern yews as ancient. It lists them as of no great age, included only because the bleeding yew draws thousands of visitors each year. The avenue is sometimes put at 600 to 700 years, a figure we could not trace to a firm source, and no girth has been recorded for the bleeding tree. Legends fill the gap. One ties the red sap to the Crucifixion; another says the tree will bleed until a Welsh prince rules again from Nevern Castle, on the hill above the village. The Pembrokeshire Coast National Park gives the tree its own page among its land of legends. St Brynach's has older witnesses than any of its yews. A carved Celtic cross from the late tenth or early eleventh century stands in the churchyard with the Vitalianus stone, inscribed in Latin and ogham, and the church itself dates from around 1380. Nevern is about 3 km east of Newport, with buses on the Fishguard to Cardigan road passing the turning.

faq.q: Why does the Nevern yew bleed?
faq.a: It oozes a dark red-brown sap from a broken stub on its trunk. Legend gives reasons, from the Crucifixion to a lost Welsh prince; the National Park asks the same question on its page about the tree.

faq.q: How old is the Bleeding Yew?
faq.a: Not documented. The avenue is sometimes put at 600 to 700 years, but the Ancient Yew Group calls these yews of no great age.

faq.q: Is it free to visit?
faq.a: Yes. It stands in the open churchyard of St Brynach's, Nevern, about 3 km from Newport, Pembrokeshire.

martindale.intro: Martindale maps one tree: the twin-trunked yew in the churchyard of old St Martin's, at the end of a quiet valley road above Ullswater. Age estimates run from 700 years to 2,000, and the Ancient Yew Group calls this one of the finest churchyard yew settings in England. Local tradition says it supplied bows for Agincourt, which nobody has proved. Free, and most easily reached by boat to Howtown and a walk up the valley.
martindale.meta_description: The Martindale Yew above Ullswater: a twin-trunked yew put at 700 to 2,000 years old in the churchyard of old St Martin's. Free to visit.
martindale.question_meta: Martindale's oldest tree is the yew at old St Martin's Church, with estimates from 700 to 2,000 years and no settled answer.
martindale.question_answer: Martindale's oldest and only mapped tree is the Martindale Yew, a European Yew (Taxus baccata) in the churchyard of old St Martin's Church, Martindale, in the Ullswater valley of the Lake District. Age estimates run from 700 to 2,000 years; the Ancient Yew Group leans to the lower end because it grows as two joined trunks.
martindale.question_context: The yew stands north-east of the little church, a female tree whose two trunks are joined only for the first few feet and measured 5.92 metres round together in 2002. One trunk is a hollow shell with a thickened rim, the other is covered in twiggy growth, and a branch about six feet up dips to the ground. The Church of England's heritage record gives about 1,300 years, a figure that sits inside the wider estimate rather than settling it. The site has been documented since 1220, and the first time the tree appears in print is 1839, when William Ford called it a picturesque yew-tree. The story that it supplied longbows for Agincourt is one the National Churches Trust calls probable but not proven. A 2018 survey found the crown in normal health, with some dead branches on the south side. There is no bus. The usual way in is the Ullswater Steamers boat to Howtown pier and a walk of about 2.5 km up the valley road; by car it is about 15 minutes from Pooley Bridge.

faq.q: How old is the Martindale Yew?
faq.a: Estimates run from 700 to 2,000 years. The Ancient Yew Group thinks the lower end more likely because the tree is two joined trunks; a church record gives about 1,300.

faq.q: Did it supply bows for Agincourt?
faq.a: That is the local story. The National Churches Trust calls it probable but not proven.

faq.q: How do you get there without a car?
faq.a: Take the Ullswater Steamers boat to Howtown pier and walk about 2.5 km up the Martindale valley road to old St Martin's.

lorton.intro: Lorton maps one tree, the yew Wordsworth called the pride of Lorton Vale. George Fox, founder of the Quakers, noted it in 1653; Coleridge was brought to see it in 1799. A storm later broke it in half, and the fallen wood became the Mayor's Chair in Cockermouth. What remains, 4.95 metres round, stands on private ground beside Hope Beck, best seen from the Pound, the village green by Whit Beck, where it has an interpretation board.
lorton.meta_description: The Lorton Yew, Wordsworth's pride of Lorton Vale, seen from the village green in High Lorton. Storm-broken, disputed in age, free to view.
lorton.question_meta: Lorton's oldest tree is the Lorton Yew, Wordsworth's pride of Lorton Vale; estimates of its age run from about 500 years to 1,200.
lorton.question_answer: Lorton's oldest and only mapped tree is the Lorton Yew, a European Yew (Taxus baccata) behind Yew Tree Hall in High Lorton, near Cockermouth in Cumbria. Local sources say at least 1,000 years and the parish history suggests about 1,200, while the Ancient Yew Group's rule of thumb would put its present trunk nearer 500 or 600.
lorton.question_context: The yew is famous for its visitors. George Fox noted it in 1653, so full of people that he feared they would break it down. Wordsworth named it the pride of Lorton Vale in his poem Yew-Trees and showed it to Coleridge in 1799. A county history of 1816 recorded the trunk at 27 feet, about 8.2 metres, but a storm in the 19th century broke the tree in half, and the wood of the fallen part was made into the Mayor's Chair in Cockermouth. In 2002 the Ancient Yew Group measured what remains at 4.95 metres, a hollow, broken female tree slowly losing branches, which is why its age is so hard to read. It stands on private ground beside Hope Beck, behind the old malt house that is now the village hall. See it from the Pound, the small public green by Whit Beck at the bridge, where the tree has its own interpretation board. A daughter tree, planted in 2004, grows at Crossgates between Low and High Lorton. The seasonal Honister Rambler bus from Keswick serves the village from spring to autumn.

faq.q: Can you visit the Lorton Yew?
faq.a: You can see it, not touch it. It stands on private ground; the view is from the Pound, the public green by Whit Beck in High Lorton, where it has an interpretation board.

faq.q: How old is the Lorton Yew?
faq.a: Estimates differ. Local sources say at least 1,000 years and the parish history about 1,200; the size of today's storm-broken trunk suggests nearer 500 or 600.

faq.q: Why is it famous?
faq.a: Wordsworth called it the pride of Lorton Vale, George Fox noted it in 1653, and Coleridge came to see it in 1799.

beltingham.intro: Beltingham maps one tree: a twisted, hollow yew held together with metal straps in the churchyard of St Cuthbert's, a hamlet on the South Tyne near Bardon Mill. It is 5.21 metres round and said locally to be at least 900 years old, a figure nobody has sourced. In 2020 it made the Woodland Trust's shortlist for England's Tree of the Year. Free, and about an hour from Newcastle by train and a short walk.
beltingham.meta_description: The Beltingham Yew in Northumberland: a strapped, hollow churchyard yew said to be 900 years old, shortlisted for Tree of the Year 2020. Free.
beltingham.question_meta: Beltingham's oldest tree is the strapped yew in St Cuthbert's churchyard, said locally to be at least 900 years old, a figure without a source.
beltingham.question_answer: Beltingham's oldest and only mapped tree is the Beltingham Yew, a European Yew (Taxus baccata) in St Cuthbert's churchyard near Bardon Mill, Northumberland. The Hexham Courant says it is said to be at least 900 years old, without naming a source; the church beside it dates from around 1500.
beltingham.question_context: The tree is easy to find because of how it is held together. Metal straps wrap the twisted, hollow trunk at about three feet and seven feet, binding two living fragments to what is left of the decaying original. The Ancient Yew Group measured it at 5.21 metres round in 2002 and recorded it as male. Two other yews grow in the churchyard, one of them 4.83 metres round. The 900-year figure is local lore. The yew group dates the church to around 1500, thinks the site likely much older, and finds the first written mention of the yew in parish records of 1828. The girth fits a tree several centuries old without proving any particular number. In 2020 the Beltingham Yew was one of ten trees shortlisted for the Woodland Trust's England Tree of the Year, one of two from the North East alongside Heaton's Shoe Tree in Newcastle. Getting there makes a day out. Take the Tyne Valley line from Newcastle to Bardon Mill, about 50 minutes, then walk about a kilometre across the South Tyne.

faq.q: How old is the Beltingham Yew?
faq.a: It is said locally to be at least 900 years old, but no source for that figure is named. The church beside it dates from around 1500.

faq.q: Why is it held with straps?
faq.a: The trunk is twisted and hollow, and metal straps at about three and seven feet bind two living fragments to the decaying original.

faq.q: How do you get there from Newcastle?
faq.a: Take the Tyne Valley line to Bardon Mill, about 50 minutes, then walk roughly a kilometre across the South Tyne to St Cuthbert's.

liverpool.intro: Liverpool's three mapped trees split between two places. In Calderstones Park, Allerton, stands the Allerton Oak, England's Tree of the Year in 2019, split, hollow, propped on metal crutches since 1907, and still dropping acorns, with a sweet chestnut almost seven metres round a short walk away. South of the city, two yews called Adam and Eve fill the cobbled courtyard of Speke Hall, a Tudor house where frames were made to protect them in 1712.
liverpool.meta_description: The Allerton Oak, England's Tree of the Year 2019, a spiralling Calderstones chestnut, and Speke Hall's Adam and Eve yews, guarded since 1712.

cardiff.intro: Cardiff's seven mapped trees are mostly in Bute Park, where one short walk passes three Glamorgan champions, the Blackfriars plane at 612 centimetres round, a Turkey oak and a ginkgo that turns gold in November, plus a 34-metre beech. A sweet chestnut there sat unrecorded until volunteers taped it in 2023. Further out, the Maiden Oak of St Fagans, never pollarded, is put at 180 to 350 years, and a tree planted in 1985 remembers Raoul Wallenberg.
cardiff.meta_description: Seven Cardiff trees: Bute Park's champion plane, Turkey oak and ginkgo, a 34m beech, the Maiden Oak of St Fagans and a Wallenberg memorial.
